reviews.text: I came into Dice Have No Eyes expecting “Balatro but with dice”. I stayed because apparently I’m a tactical genius who simply chooses to roll three 1s in a row for strategic reasons. This game absolutely nails that “one more run” roguelike brain poison. The dice mechanics feel super satisfying, and the trinket/build combinations get gloriously unhinged once you start understanding how everything interacts. Every run slowly transforms from “surely I can bank this level” into “I have created a machine powered entirely by greed and bad decisions”. And unlike normal dice games, this isn’t really about luck. Anyone can roll sixes. Real skill is confidently locking in a terrible play and then blaming probability afterward. The atmosphere is also weirdly charming in the best way possible; creepy little dice creatures, surreal visuals, ominous vibes, and a general feeling that the game itself is judging your gambling addiction. Having played over 10 hours during the private playtest, I can honestly say the devs cooked. The balancing kept getting better, new interactions constantly surprised me, and every session ended with me saying “okay ONE more run”. If you like Balatro, dice-building roguelikes, or games that make you feel simultaneously brilliant and cursed, this is an easy recommendation. May God guide your dice.

Dice Have No Eyes is a roguelike strategy game developed by Franek and Max Cahill and published by Franek that builds an entire experience around risk, greed, and the dangerous temptation to keep pushing your luck. At its foundation, the concept feels deceptively simple. Players roll dice to earn points, gather upgrades, and survive increasingly difficult encounters. Beneath that straightforward setup lies a surprisingly engaging loop driven by probability management, build experimentation, and the constant tension between playing safely and chasing something greater. The game's biggest strength comes from understanding player psychology. Early decisions feel manageable. Roll carefully, secure rewards, and slowly build momentum. Success creates confidence, and confidence creates risk. Before long, every run becomes a battle not only against the game's challenges but against your own willingness to gamble everything for one more opportunity. Dice Have No Eyes turns restraint into a mechanic just as important as strategy. The progression structure follows roguelike principles while shaping them around dice manipulation and score optimization. Every run offers opportunities to strengthen builds through upgrades, modifiers, and strange combinations that dramatically alter how progression unfolds. Small improvements eventually evolve into powerful synergies capable of transforming an average run into something wildly effective. Discovering those combinations becomes one of the game's most satisfying elements. Variety plays an important role in maintaining long-term appeal. The game introduces a large collection of upgrades, trinkets, consumables, and spells that continually reshape strategy possibilities. Runs rarely feel identical because available tools constantly push players toward experimentation. Some upgrades reward safer approaches built around consistency while others encourage reckless strategies focused entirely on massive rewards. The freedom to pursue different styles gives the game impressive replay value. Companion systems further expand build possibilities. Different allies provide distinct effects that influence progression in meaningful ways, creating another layer of strategic planning beyond raw probability management. Choosing how companion abilities interact with upgrades and dice modifiers creates satisfying opportunities for optimization without overwhelming accessibility. One of the game's strongest achievements is how effectively it creates tension from simple mechanics. Few experiences generate stress quite like staring at an excellent run while deciding whether one more roll will lead to victory or complete disaster. Dice Have No Eyes consistently weaponizes greed against the player. Strong momentum encourages increasingly dangerous decisions, and the game understands exactly how to tempt players toward mistakes. Failure becomes part of the appeal rather than a source of frustration. Losses often feel self-inflicted rather than unfair. Runs collapse because players chase opportunities beyond what caution allows. That structure creates a surprisingly addictive cycle where defeat rarely discourages another attempt. Instead, failure becomes a lesson and motivation for future experimentation. The game's presentation complements its unusual identity well. Dice Have No Eyes embraces strange humor and surreal creativity rather than taking itself too seriously. Item descriptions, upgrades, and world design frequently lean into absurd ideas that give the experience personality beyond mechanical systems alone. The strange tone keeps progression entertaining while helping the game separate itself from more serious strategy-focused roguelikes. Visual design favors readability and style over technical complexity. Information remains understandable even during more chaotic moments while effects reinforce progression without creating unnecessary clutter. The interface communicates important details efficiently, allowing players to focus on planning rather than fighting menus. Humor also plays a surprisingly valuable role. Games built heavily around randomness can become frustrating when luck turns against players repeatedly. Dice Have No Eyes counters that problem through personality and self-awareness. Strange design choices and playful presentation soften difficult losses while preserving tension. The game feels fully aware that it occasionally encourages terrible decisions and quietly enjoys watching players make them anyway. As an Early Access project, there are naturally areas still developing. Additional content and balancing improvements continue shaping the long-term experience. Some players who prefer heavily deterministic strategy systems may occasionally struggle with moments where randomness influences outcomes significantly. However, luck is not an obstacle to the design. It is the foundation supporting everything else. The game works best when players embrace uncertainty rather than attempting to eliminate it completely. Planning matters. Smart decisions matter. Understanding probabilities matters. But ultimately, Dice Have No Eyes thrives because it constantly asks one dangerous question: are you satisfied with what you have, or do you want more? Franek and Max Cahill have created a roguelike that transforms simple mechanics into something consistently tense and rewarding. By combining build experimentation, strategic risk management, and unpredictable progression systems, Dice Have No Eyes creates an experience that feels easy to understand but difficult to master. It succeeds because it understands something many strategy games overlook. Players often become their own greatest obstacle. Dice Have No Eyes simply gives them enough freedom to prove it. Rating: 8/10

I've always enjoyed games in which you weigh continuing for more points against the risk of losing what you have, and Dice Have No Eyes largely revolves around this mechanic. Unlike similar games, you will always have an unlimited number of tries to raise your score and can continue long after surpassing the goal. The round only ends when you either choose to walk away or push too far and lose it all. Most dice in the game have a pink 1 which gives you a strike when rolled. Too many strikes and you lose all your accumulated unbanked points and one of your attempts for the round. Striking out on your final attempt will end the run and forfeit any unbanked meta currency. There are dice in the shop with extra pink sides, giving you extra chances to fail. Dice also have a health limit and some will take damage instead of giving you a strike when rolling 1. While these will not give you a strike, once they shatter you will be down a die for the round which makes it significantly more difficult to earn points, and you lose the opportunity to sell a die once it breaks. There are items that increase the number of strikes it takes to lose, but every die is a d6 and the odds of landing on any one side generally remain the same. Another noteworthy mechanic is the "instant wipe." Get a strike on every selected die and you will go bust even if you had more strikes remaining. This makes rolling a single die to fix a straight super dangerous. There is also a "momentum" mechanic that raises your multiplier for every hand you turn in before banking your points. Together, you are generally better off submitting every hand you get rather than aiming for specific things. Boss stages shake this up with effects like damaging your dice every time you submit a hand or giving negative points to certain types of hand. Dice Have No Eyes has an interconnected node system for its meta unlocks. Each node has a title such as "More Spells" which obviously adds more spells to the shop's selection. However, you won't actually know what those spells are until you spend your stars to unlock the node. Thankfully the shop is divided into distinct sections, so extra snacks won't make it harder to find trinkets. I never really got a super synergistic build going, but I also never felt like I needed one to succeed as good management of the core systems seems to give plenty of points. Most unlocks aside from characters have relatively low requirements. Characters require gold stars earned from winning a full run, so that can take a while. Between the two the game does not feel super grindy but will take some effort to unlock everything. The game also has some whimsical charm to it. Certain items take effect by feeding them to a specific die, and when you hold such an item your dice will chase it with their mouths open. The title screen allows you to click any option, but you also have the choice to roll a die and start a match if it rolls a 6 or quit if it rolls a 1. If you abuse an unfair die, an entity calling itself "God" will appear and destroy it. The game has a distinct atmosphere that stands out from its more serious competitors, and I appreciate it. Dice Have No Eyes is a game I thoroughly enjoy and I can see it being my go-to for casual score-attack play. It has some charming quirks while its core gameplay is simple yet very solid. I would recommend this game to anyone who is willing to go double or nothing on a coin flip.

The epitome of risk vs. reward. Unlike a lot of other games in this genre, where you only get a set number of rerolls per turn (see Balatro, Slice & Dice, and CloverPit), Dice Have No Eyes lets you (theoretically) reroll as much as you want on any given turn. I'm a huge fan of games that let you choose to play it safe or continually double down, and that is a central theme of this game. The gameplay looks relatively simple on the surface, revolving around rolling dice to score poker hands, but there's a surprising amount of decision-making involved with every reroll, which only increases (or decreases) depending on how you shape your build. I've had runs where I tunneled hard into rolling for Pair/Two Pair/Three Pair because of my trinket choice, and others where I went flexed around Full House and Five of a Kind due to the consumable spells and snacks I was offered. The various characters and their powers also enable more unique combos and playstyles, like Wizard being able to easily take advantage of the coin flipping mechanic due to their shield power. Many other options open up as you progress due to the extensive meta-progression unlcock tree, which contains new characters, trinkets, snacks, and spells to try out in future runs. Overall, for an Early Access title, this game is incredibly polished. It has an amazing art style/aesthetic, and I appreciate the devs supporting indie musicians by including their incredible music tracks in this game. The devs are also super active in their Discord, open to feedback and suggestions from players, and seem to have a clear vision for what content they want to add and how they want to balance the game, which bodes well for the game's future and the eventual end product it will turn out to be. 10/10 would highly recommend giving Dice Have No Eyes a shot if you are a fan of deckbuilder/dicebuilder roguelites!
